title: The Cloud of Unknowing (14th century)
hook: an anonymous English guide: God is reached by love, not by thinking

segments.voice: Yesterday, centering prayer: one sacred word and a gentle return. Your line was consent to his presence. Did you call your mind back without scolding it? Today, the old book those monks leaned on. Day two hundred forty-five.

A swimming manual has never kept anyone afloat. A list of reasons to love someone is not the love. Some things can't be reached by thinking. Somewhere in England, in the 1300s, a writer whose name we'll never know sat down to teach a young person how to pray, and made exactly this point about God. The book is short, strange, and funny in places. Its title is today's word.
screen: `YOU CAN'T THINK YOUR WAY INTO LOVE.` → `ENGLAND, THE 1300S.` → `A WRITER WITH NO NAME.`

segments.voice: The Cloud of Unknowing was written in Middle English, the English of Chaucer's time, by an author who hid his name on purpose. Some readers guess he was a priest, perhaps a Carthusian monk. Nobody knows. First, the two clouds. When you turn toward God, he says, you find a darkness between you and God, a cloud of unknowing. Your mind can't get through it. So you put everything else, all your thoughts, even good ones, beneath you in a cloud of forgetting. Second, the key. God can't be reached by thinking, he says, but God can be reached by love. He puts it in a line of two halves: by love God may be gotten and held, but by thought never. Your mind can know about God. Only love can touch God. Third, the dart. So what do you do in the cloud? You send up what he calls a sharp dart of longing love. Keep it short. He suggests one word, even one syllable, like God, or love, and says to fasten it to your heart. A short prayer, he says, pierces heaven. His own picture: someone whose house is on fire doesn't make a speech. They shout one word, fire. Fourth, the humor. He warns against people who strain so hard at prayer that they pull strange faces and twist themselves about. Relax, he says. Don't force it. Our last two weeks have walked through ways of praying: contemplation, lectio divina, the examen, imagination, the Hours, Compline, the Jesus Prayer, a kitchen, a sacred word, and now a cloud. Tomorrow, a saint builds a castle.
screen: `A CLOUD OF UNKNOWING ABOVE.` · `BY LOVE, NOT BY THOUGHT.` · `A SHARP DART OF LONGING LOVE.` · `DON'T STRAIN. DON'T FORCE IT.` · then, large: `SHORT PRAYER PIERCES HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send a short dart of love. Settle. Let your thoughts drift down beneath you, even the good ones. If you pray, choose one word, God or love, and send it upward, short and whole, whenever you feel the pull. No explaining. If you don't pray, send the word toward whatever you love most, and let the word do the loving. The bell holds the time.
The Cloud of Unknowing. An anonymous English guide from the 1300s: God can't be held by thinking, only by love. Today's word.

Your line: by love, not thought. Today, when you catch yourself overthinking someone you love, stop analyzing and do one kind thing for them instead. Day two hundred forty-five. Two weeks of ways of praying, done.

howItsDone: Some Catholics read The Cloud of Unknowing as a guide to silent, wordless prayer, repeating a single short word like God or love as a movement of the heart, and it underlies modern methods such as centering prayer.

fork.setup: you're sitting in prayer, and all you find is darkness, a cloud your mind can't get through. what does the book say to do?
options: give up; this prayer isn't for you.
send up a short dart of longing love.
fork.reveal: love, not thought, gets through the cloud. keep it short: one word, even one syllable.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mystical book with a spooky title.
what it means: a practical guide: God is beyond the mind, so you reach God by short, whole acts of love.
what a scholar hears: Middle English, 14th century, anonymous; it draws on the tradition of Pseudo-Dionysius, who taught that God is known in darkness.

notes: All lines from the Cloud are paraphrased (the well-known 'by love may he be gotten and holden; but by thought never' is in modernized editions whose exact wording varies); the screen line 'SHORT PRAYER PIERCES HEAVEN' is a paraphrase of ch. 37–38. Confirm chapter numbers.
The 'fire' illustration: the Cloud itself uses the image of someone crying out 'fire' in a single word (ch. 37); confirm.
Authorship: anonymous; a Carthusian or a country priest are common scholarly guesses. Stated as uncertain.
Humor about straining (strange faces and bodily contortions): paraphrased from the chapters on false contemplatives; confirm the images are in the text.
